newsitem.title: UK: International LPG firm in all centres, good buying.
newsitem.headline: International LPG firm in all centres, good buying.

text.p: International Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) prices remained firm in all major centres this week, with buying seen for petrochemical, storage and normal domestic usage at high prices even though demand is traditionally low at this point of the summer.
The northwest European market has seen continued good demand for propane, and some of this is being met from Algeria, a trader said.
"North Sea availabilities are fairly tight for June with few sellers," he said, adding that cargoes of 10,000 tonnes to 20,000 tonnes are being discussed in the low $190's a tonne cif NWE.

European propane demand is coming from three sources. Petrochemical buyers are picking up material, some of which has been seen coming from Algeria; then there is demand from traders who have short positions into petrochemical users; and there is also demand from inland users buying to cover domestic heating and cooking requirements.

"Propane is roughly at parity with naphtha," said a dealer. "For just cracking marginal tonnes, petchems would require cheaper feedstock than propane, so the demand shows there are other people in the market than just petchem buyers."

But while propane demand is strong and levels firm, butane remains thin, with no cargo trades seen for several weeks. A seller is moving a 40,000 tonne mixed cargo to the US Gulf Coast, including a high proportion of isobutane which commands a high premium in the US over Europe, in the next few days. But this was sold some time ago, and there has been little interest since then.

BP on Friday announced its posted prices, the BP Agreed Price or BPAP, on Friday, at $173 a tonne for propane and $159 a tonne for butane. Traders had said the market had been relatively quiet towards the end of the week as players awaited the announcement of BPAP.

But there was no word by the end of the week on the other posted prices, Saudi Aramco's Contract Price (CP), against which most east of Suez business is done, or Sonatrach's price for Algerian LPG. Traders said the CP was expected on Saturday, while the Sonatrach price was likely to be announced after the weekend.

In the Mediterranean, maintenance work on the storage cavern at Lavera, the main LPG terminal in southern France, is keeping the terminal closed from June 10-20, a trader said. As a result the Mediterranean market is temporarily quiet, but there is expected to be an upturn in business towards the end of the month.

But a trader said there were rumours that 10,000 tonnes of propane from the North Sea had been sold at a price in the low to mid $190's a tonne cif Lavera, and that another cargo of 20,000 tonnes from Algeria had been done at the same price, both for end June delivery. These rumours were not confirmed, he added.

In Asia, premiums over the CP have started to rise, partly in anticipation of a lower CP in June, partly because demand is increasing, and partly because of soaring freight rates. A mixed propane/butane cargo was reported done at around CP +$28 a tonne, with offers now heard coming from over CP + $30 a tonne. It was not clear if this was for a 20,000 tonne or 40,000 tonne cargo.

Freight from the Middle East Gulf to Japan is assessed at between $25 and $28 a tonne, with a premium of around $1.50 a tonne for delivery to South Korea. A trader said that one vessel had been fixed at $28 a tonne from Das Island, but this was considered unusually high because Das is considered a "difficult" port.

Japanese buyers are beginning to look for storage tonnes to keep in stock for next winter. They have long been waiting for the optimum moment to buy, when both the CP and the premium to it are at their lowest, and a Japanese trader said that buyers are now beginning to say July is likely to be the best time.

But meantime levels remain firm. Much depends on the acceptances to nominations that Saudi Aramco announces in its June loading programme. "If there are excess cargoes after the acceptances, the price may collapse," the Japanese trader said. "But if not, it will continue to be bullish," he added.

South Korean company Kedco has issued a buying tender for one full cargo of 43,000 tonnes of propane, to be delivered to the terminal of Pyongtaek between July 11 and 25. Bids close on June 3, to be valid until June 5.

But India's IOC had cancelled its one-year term tender for 540,000 tonnes of LPG. "It was cancelled because the requirement was not there," said a source close to the company. "IOC has plans to issue a new one-year tender but the details are still being worked out."

The US market has been steady and quiet. Propane towards the end of the week was discussed at between 35.25 cents and 35.50 cents a gallon at the Mont Belvieu, Texas hub, while Butane at Conway, Kansas was talked at 37.50/37.75 cents a gallon.
